Introduction
The Business Architecture defines the foundational structure of how a statistical organization delivers its mission within the modern data ecosystem. It provides a coherent view of the organization’s functions, value streams, stakeholders, and capabilities that enable the production, management, and dissemination of official statistics and data services. Within the SAF, the business architecture translates the high-level strategic motivations—expressed in the motivation layer—into an operational model that guides transformation, modernization, and alignment across the statistical system.
At its core, the Business Architecture captures what the organization does, for whom, and how value is created and delivered through its business processes and capabilities. It articulates the end-to-end value chain of statistical production and data management, encompassing activities such as data acquisition, processing, analysis, dissemination, and stewardship. These activities are represented through value streams aligned with the Generic Statistical Business Process Model (GSBPM) and supported by reusable, interoperable business capabilities that form the backbone of the statistical enterprise.
The SAF Business Architecture is developed using TOGAF ADM principles and modeled in ArchiMate, ensuring traceability from strategic intent to implementation. It establishes a common language and structure to describe and compare the operational models of statistical organizations across countries, enabling collaboration, capability sharing, and architectural alignment within the international statistical community. Each capability within the architecture describes a stable “what” of the business—an ability that remains consistent even when processes, technologies, or organizational structures evolve—thereby supporting long-term modernization and resilience.
In the context of SAF, the Business Architecture also acts as a bridge between policy and implementation. It defines the organizational context within which new technologies (e.g., data fabrics, data spaces, AI-driven analytics) and emerging business models (e.g., data sharing ecosystems, federated infrastructures, secure processing environments) can be embedded. This ensures that innovation is introduced coherently and sustainably, without fragmenting existing statistical processes or undermining governance, quality, and trust.
The architecture distinguishes between core, supporting, and enabling business domains. Core domains represent the essential statistical production and data lifecycle functions—those directly linked to the generation and dissemination of statistical outputs. Supporting domains include governance, quality management, and compliance, ensuring that statistical outputs meet ethical, methodological, and legal standards. Enabling domains cover digital and organizational capabilities such as IT management, data infrastructure, and human capital that sustain and empower statistical operations. Together, these domains ensure that the organization’s business functions align with national strategies, international standards, and the UNECE modernization principles.
Finally, the Business Architecture provides a foundation for alignment with other frameworks and reference models, such as the Common Statistical Production Architecture (CSPA), Common Statistical Data Architecture (CSDA), and the European Statistical System Reference Architecture (ESS-RA). By positioning the SAF Business Architecture as an integrative layer, it allows statistical organizations to map their internal business functions against internationally recognized models, facilitating interoperability, benchmarking, and shared capability development across borders.
In summary, the Business Architecture within the Statistical Architecture Framework defines the structural and functional essence of the statistical organization. It provides a unified view of business intent, functions, and capabilities, ensuring that modernization initiatives are business-driven, strategically aligned, and technically coherent. It is the blueprint through which the statistical enterprise can evolve towards a data-centric, service-oriented, and collaborative future—anchored in trust, quality, and value for society.
